title: Library Compatibility and Versioning knowledge check

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a declaration file?
options: It replaces the runtime JavaScript implementation.
It proves a package is secure.
It describes the types of existing JavaScript APIs without providing their runtime implementation.
questions.answer_key: It describes the types of existing JavaScript APIs without providing their runtime implementation.
questions.explanation: Declaration files describe APIs and should be tested against real consumers and supported versions.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Library Compatibility and Versioning”?
options: A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with semantic versioning for type contracts and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with semantic versioning for type contracts and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Semantic versioning for type contracts”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Library Compatibility and Versioning”?
options: Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check breaking type changes, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume testing types across supported environments is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
questions.answer_key: Check breaking type changes, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Breaking type changes”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
